query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Selective gas-induced oxidation (or reduction) of reactive elements (especially Cr and Ti) at grain boundaries governs degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, leading to local elemental depletion, brittle secondary phase formation, and eventually catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC matrix and no significant secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the gas atmosphere by exposing identical specimens to an oxidizing environment (high-purity O2 or O2-rich air) versus a reducing environment (H2- or CO-rich gas) at a fixed elevated temperature (900–1100°C) and controlled exposure duration.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure at 900–1100°C under well-controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for durations sufficient to induce measurable microstructural evolution but not complete transformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of continuous oxide layers or reduction products at grain boundaries that cause local depletion of Cr and Ti, promoting the nucleation of brittle secondary phases or σ-type precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, rapid surface and grain boundary oxidation of Cr and Ti leads to their depletion from critical regions, resulting in brittle secondary phase formation and weakened grain boundary cohesion that eventually triggers catastrophic failure. In contrast, reducing environments suppress these surface reactions, mitigating degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens exposed to oxidizing atmospheres will exhibit significant grain boundary oxidation, evident Cr/Ti depletion, the emergence of brittle oxide or secondary phases, and a measurable decrease in mechanical integrity relative to both the as-built state and specimens exposed to reducing conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy state characterized by a uniform FCC matrix with balanced elemental distribution and no pre-existing detrimental precipitates.
generation.boundary: Exposure conducted at temperatures between 900°C and 1100°C, under distinct oxidizing versus reducing gas atmospheres, within exposure times that allow surface and grain boundary changes but avoid complete phase transformation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative kinetics of selective oxidation/reduction and the exact threshold for critical elemental depletion are not fully established and may vary with slight compositional or microstructural variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose identical as-built HEA specimens to controlled oxidizing (O2-rich) and reducing (H2/CO-rich) atmospheres at 900–1100°C for a fixed duration. Characterize the specimens pre- and post-exposure using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) with elemental mapping (EDS) to detect grain boundary oxidation and secondary phase formation, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness, fracture toughness) to assess degradation.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental analysis (measuring Cr and Ti depletion)
Identification and quantification of oxide or secondary phase precipitates
Mechanical property changes (reduction in hardness/fracture toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens exposed to oxidizing conditions do not exhibit significant grain boundary oxidation, no detectable depletion of Cr and Ti, and no corresponding decrease in mechanical performance relative to both the as-built baseline and reducing atmosphere specimens, then the hypothesis that gas-induced selective oxidation governs degradation leading to catastrophic failure is falsified.

Unlike the classical Cantor alloys obtained by casting technology, the alloy obtained by SLM did not require prolonged exposure to high temperatures to produce secondary phase precipitation. SLM technology with Nitrogen protective atmosphere induced a fine secondary phases precipitation of nitrides and intermetallic phases in the as-built state. The cold-rolled plus annealed FCC matrix became unstable and secondary phases precipitated. The observed precipitation was made of tetragonal Cr-rich σ phase and of mixed Cr-(Fe, Mn, Co, Ni)-nitrides which nucleated at the triple points. The size of the σ phase precipitates increased with annealing temperature. When the annealing temperature was below the recrystallization temperature, the size of precipitates was small due to a low diffusion rate and confined at the grain boundaries of the as-built dendritic structure. When the temperature exceeded 1323 K, the σ phase dissolved and the alloy substantially returned to single phase with near equiatomic composition. σ phase and nitride precipitations yielded a significant alloy hardening only at room temperature and for annealing up to 923 K, that is, below recrystallization temperature. AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys largely focused on intrinsic phase transformations and mechanical behavior in as‐built or thermally aged microstructures. For instance, initial studies examined microstructural evolution and creep mechanisms in decoupled conditions (e.g., under vacuum or inert atmosphere), while more recent work (such as PMC9969177) has employed reactive atomistic simulations to reveal how corrosive environments (high‐temperature/pressure water) can alter deformation modes via surface oxidation. Similarly, studies on SLM‐made HEAs (e.g., PMC9414008) noted that processing atmospheres (such as nitrogen protection) can induce secondary precipitates, though without a clear decoupling of oxidizing vs reducing effects. Overall, the research trajectory has been from characterizing intrinsic phase and defect evolution to beginning to probe environmental influences on microstructure under high-temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: What remains unresolved is a testable, mechanistic understanding of how exposure to different gas atmospheres (oxidizing versus reducing) specifically drives degradation in additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloys. In particular, the controlled link between gas composition, surface-scale selective oxidation or reduction of reactive elements (e.g., Cr and Ti), ensuing elemental redistribution or phase evolution, and the onset of catastrophic failure has not been isolated and verified.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the gas atmosphere by exposing identical as-built specimens to defined oxidizing (e.g., high-purity O2 or O2-rich air) versus reducing (e.g., H2 or CO-rich) environments at a fixed elevated temperature range (e.g., 900–1100°C) and for controlled durations. Monitor microstructural evolution (using in-situ or post-exposure advanced characterization techniques) to detect selective oxidation/reduction effects, phase segregations, and element depletion at grain boundaries relative to an inert baseline.
decision.why: This approach is the natural next step because previous studies have hinted at environment-induced changes in microstructure through reactive simulations and incidental observations in AM alloys. By precisely controlling the gas composition, one can directly test the hypothesis that selective surface reactions (oxidation or reduction) lead to localized element depletion or secondary phase formation, which then governs degradation and eventual catastrophic failure. The clear experimental lever (gas atmosphere) provides a falsification criterion: if no measurable microstructural or mechanical deviations from the baseline are observed, the hypothesis linking gas-induced chemical reactions with degradation can be refuted.
